title: Behavioral Activation

learn.summary: Behavioral activation — originally a component of CBT that trials (notably Jacobson's 1996 dismantling study) found works about as well as the full package for depression — inverts folk wisdom: action precedes motivation, not the other way around. Low mood shrinks activity, which removes reward and mastery, which lowers mood further; BA breaks the spiral by scheduling values-based activity regardless of feeling like it. Waiting to feel like it is the trap itself.

do: Schedule one small pleasant activity and one small mastery activity for specific times this week. Do them regardless of mood; rate mood before/after each.

children.title: Action Before Motivation

learn.summary: The motivation myth says feel → do; the evidence says do → feel. Mood follows behavior with a lag, so the working rule is 'outside-in': move the body, start the task for five minutes, and let motivation catch up — it usually does, because starting removes the largest friction. Depression whispers 'wait until you feel ready'; BA's entire insight is that ready arrives after you begin.

do: Pick one task you have been waiting to feel motivated for. Use a 5-minute timer rule today: start for just five minutes, permission to stop after. Record whether you continued.

children.title: Values as Compass

learn.summary: ACT distinguishes values (directions you keep traveling: being a caring friend, learning, health) from goals (destinations you reach and finish). BA works best when scheduled activities connect to values, not just pleasure — mowing a lonely neighbor's lawn beats a third episode of anything, in mood-per-hour terms. Values also survive failure: you can act on 'being a good friend' on a terrible day when every goal feels impossible.

do: Write your top three values as directions (not goals). For each, schedule one 15-minute action this week that expresses it.

children.title: Activity Scheduling

learn.summary: BA's workhorse tool: log current activities with mood ratings to see what actually lifts or sinks you (data often surprises — scrolling rates worse than people predict, chores rate better), then deliberately schedule a balanced diet of pleasure and mastery activities into specific calendar slots. Specificity is the active ingredient: 'walk Tuesday 6pm from the front door' gets done; 'exercise more' does not. Grade tasks down until the first step is nearly impossible to fail.

do: Track activities and hourly mood (1–10) for two days. Then schedule next week to include more of your top-3 mood raisers.

children.title: Tiny Habits

learn.summary: BJ Fogg's Stanford model: behavior happens when motivation, ability, and prompt converge — and since motivation is unreliable, shrink the behavior until it needs almost none (one push-up, floss one tooth) and anchor it to an existing routine ('after I pour coffee, I...'). Celebration immediately after locks it in. James Clear's habit-stacking is the same architecture; both beat willpower because they never depend on it.

do: Install one tiny habit this week using the recipe 'After I [existing routine], I will [30-second version of new behavior]' — and track a 7-day streak.
